1.?

The point (a,b) lies on the curve y=x3. Which of the following points must lie on y=2(x+2)3?

E
Sat, Jun 14th @ 3:43 PM|Elapsed: 9:42Correct

Method 1

To plot y=2(x+2)3, we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph y=x3.

  • Then, we shift the graph horizontally by 2 units to the left and get the graph of y=(x+2)3. After this transformation, the point (a,b) will be mapped to the point (a−2,b).

  • Finally, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of 2 parallel to the y -axis and get the graph of y=2(x+2)3. After this transformation, the point (a−2,b) will be mapped to the point (a−2,2b).

Method 2

Since the point (a,b) lies on the graph of y=x3, we have that a3=b.

Now consider the graph of y=2(x+2)3. Substituting x=a−2, we get

y=2(a−2+2)3=2a3=2b.

Therefore, the point (a−2,2b) must lie on y=2(x+2)3.

2.?

The point (a,b) lies on the curve y=x. Which of the following points must lie on y=x−1−1?

E
Sat, Jun 14th @ 3:44 PM|Elapsed: 0:37Correct

Method 1

To plot y=x−1−1, we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph y=x.

  • Then, we shift the graph horizontally by 1 unit to the right and get the graph of y=x−1. After this transformation, the point (a,b) will be mapped to the point (a+1,b).

  • Finally, we shift the result vertically by 1 unit down and obtain the graph of y=x−1−1. After this transformation, the point (a+1,b) will be mapped to the point (a+1,b−1).

Method 2

Since the point (a,b) lies on the graph of y=x, we have that a=b.

Now consider the graph of y=x−1−1. Substituting x=a+1, we get

y=a+1−1−1=a−1=b−1.

Therefore, the point (a+1,b−1) must lie on y=x−1−1.

3.?

The point (0,4) lies on the curve y=f(x)+2. Which of the following points must lie on y=−f(x)−3?

M
Sat, Jun 14th @ 3:53 PM|Elapsed: 0:40Correct

Method 1

To plot y=−f(x)−3, we apply the following steps:

  • First, take the graph y=f(x)+2.

  • Then, we shift the graph vertically by 2 unit down and get the graph of y=f(x). After this transformation, the point (0,4) will be mapped to the point (0,4−2)=(0,2).

  • Next, we reflect the result across the x-axis and get the graph of y=−f(x). After this transformation, the point (0,2) will be mapped to the point (0,−(2))=(0,−2).

  • Finally, shift the result vertically by 3 units down and obtain the graph of y=−f(x)−3. After this transformation, the point (0,−2) will be mapped to the point (0,−2−3)=(0,−5).

Method 2

Since the point (0,4) lies on the graph of y=f(x)+2, we have that

f(0)+2=4⟹f(0)=2.

Now consider the graph of y=−f(x)−3. Substituting x=0, we get

y=−f(0)−3=−2−3=−5.

Therefore, the point (0,−5) must lie on y=−f(x)−3.

4.?

The point (0,3) lies on the curve y=f(x−1). Which of the following points must lie on y=f(x)+2?

H
Sat, Jun 14th @ 4:04 PM|Elapsed: 11:07Correct

Method 1

We first find a point corresponding to (0,3) on y=f(x). Then, we find a corresponding point on y=f(x)+2:

  • To plot the graph of y=f(x), we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph y=f(x−1).

    • Then, we shift the graph horizontally 1 unit to the left and get the graph of y=f(x). After this transformation, the point (0,3) will be mapped to the point (0−1,3)=(−1,3).

  • Next, to plot the graph of y=f(x)+2, we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph y=f(x).

    • Next, we shift the result vertically by 2 units up and obtain the graph of y=f(x)+2. After this transformation, the point (−1,3) will be mapped to the point (−1,3+2)=(−1,5).

Method 2

Since the point (0,3) lies on the graph of y=f(x−1), we have that

f(0−1)=3⟹f(−1)=3.

Now consider the graph of y=f(x)+2. Substituting x=−1, we get

y=f(−1)+2=3+2=5.

Therefore, the point (−1,5) must lie on y=f(x)+2.

5.?

The diagram above shows the local minimum and maximum of the function y=f(x). What is the local maximum of y=3f(x2)?

E
Sat, Jun 14th @ 4:17 PM|Elapsed: 10:38Incorrect

Notice that the graph of y=3f(x2) can be obtained from the graph of y=f(x) by

  • stretching it by a scale factor of 2 parallel to the x-axis, and then

  • stretching it by a scale factor of 3 parallel to the y-axis.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the x-axis, the combined transformation maps the local maximum of y=f(x) to the local maximum of y=3f(x2). So, we need to find the image of (−2,−1), the local maximum of y=f(x), under the transformation.

To plot y=3f(x2), we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph y=f(x) that passes through (−2,−1).

  • Then, we stretch the graph along the x-axis by a scale factor of 2 and get the graph of y=f(x2). After this transformation, the point (−2,−1) will be mapped to the point
    (2⋅(−2),−1)=(−4,−1).

  • Finally, we stretch the result along the y-axis by a scale factor of 3 and get the graph of y=3f(x2). After this transformation, the point (−4,−1) will be mapped to the point (−4,3⋅(−1))=(−4,−3).

Therefore, the local maximum of y=3f(x2) is (−4,−3).

6.?

The diagram above shows the global minimum and maximum of the function y=f(x). What is the global minimum of y=2f(x)+5?

E
Sat, Jun 14th @ 4:29 PM|Elapsed: 9:04Correct

Notice that the graph of y=2f(x)+5 can be obtained from the graph of y=f(x) by

  • stretching it by a scale factor of 2 parallel to the y-axis, and then

  • translating it by 5 units up.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the x-axis, the combined transformation maps the global minimum of y=f(x) to the global minimum of y=2f(x)+5. So, we need to find the image of (4,−5), the global minimum of y=f(x), under the transformation.

To plot y=2f(x)+5, we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph y=f(x) that passes through (4,−5).

  • Then, we stretch the graph along the y-axis by a scale factor of 2 and get the graph of y=2f(x). After this transformation, the point (4,−5) will be mapped to the point
    (4,2⋅(−5))=(4,−10).

  • Finally, we shift the result parallel to the y-axis by 5 units up and get the graph of y=2f(x)+5. After this transformation, the point (4,−10) will be mapped to the point (4,−10+5)=(4,−5).

Therefore, the global minimum of y=2f(x)+5 is (4,−5).

7.?

The diagram above shows the global minimum and maximum of the function y=f(x). What is the global minimum of y=f(3x)+4?

E
Sat, Jun 14th @ 4:43 PM|Elapsed: 14:10Correct

Notice that the graph of y=f(3x)+4 can be obtained from the graph of y=f(x) by

  • stretching it by a scale factor of 13 parallel to the x-axis, and then

  • translating it by 4 units up.

Since these transformations do not flip the graph across the x-axis, the combined transformation maps the global minimum of y=f(x) to the global minimum of y=f(3x)+4. So, we need to find the image of (15,−5), the global minimum of y=f(x), under the transformation.

To plot y=f(3x)+4, we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph y=f(x) that passes through (15,−5).

  • Then, we stretch the result along the x-axis by a scale factor of 13 and get the graph of y=f(3x). After this transformation, the point (15,−5) will be mapped to the point
    (13⋅15,−5)=(5,−5).

  • Finally, we shift the graph vertically by 4 units up and get the graph of y=f(3x)+4. After this transformation, the point (5,−5) will be mapped to the point (5,−5+4)=(5,−1).

Therefore, the global minimum of y=f(3x)+4 is (5,−1).
